title: Workspace Reflow
user: Knowledge workers with low vision who need to read dense web-app panes without losing the task context around them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A knowledge worker asks which tools will make a transition to low vision workable; replies point to screen readers but not a useful intermediate reading workflow.
A screen-reader user asks for an automatically enabled flat, decoration-free rendering mode because the current accessibility flag is undiscoverable.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 requests describe the same gap between ordinary zoom and full screen-reader mode; it blocks routine reading in information-dense tools.
current_workaround: Browser zoom, OS magnifier, reader mode, or switching completely to a screen reader.
incumbents_and_gap: ZoomText, macOS Zoom, and reader modes magnify or strip a whole page. They do not let a user pin one selected app region into a large, keyboard-first, semantically reflowed reading pane while retaining surrounding context.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension: user selects a DOM region, opens a high-contrast reflow pane with font/line-width presets and keyboard sentence navigation, and saves a per-site rule. Non-goals: screen-reader replacement, OCR, or remote page processing.
success_measure: In a 14-day pilot, 60% of participants save rules for at least three work sites and rate at least 80% of reflows readable without additional zoom.
monetization: one-time — a local accessibility utility should not charge a recurring fee for basic reading access.
constraints: All DOM processing stays on device; do not bypass paywalls or DRM; preserve keyboard focus and ARIA semantics; support a one-key escape hatch.
why_distinct: It is contextual reflow for a chosen live workspace region, not another magnifier or generic reader mode.

title: Caption Confidence
user: People with high-frequency hearing loss who use captions and need uncertain words made easy to catch without replaying every line.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker specifically wants captions to bold words likely to be misheard because of high-frequency hearing loss.
A Subtitle Edit user reports bad speech-to-text output with no warning, demonstrating that a visible reliability signal is missing from caption workflows.

recurrence: A direct accessibility request plus a separate caption-authoring failure report; a single missed word can change the meaning of dialogue or instruction.
current_workaround: Replay scenes, turn on generic captions, or manually inspect a transcript.
incumbents_and_gap: YouTube and Netflix expose styling controls, while Subtitle Edit helps author files. None offers a user-controlled uncertainty/important-word emphasis layer for user-supplied VTT/SRT or supported HTML5 video.
smallest_useful_product: Local web app/extension that imports VTT/SRT or reads an exposed HTML5 track, highlights user-defined sound-confusion pairs and low-confidence timing gaps, and offers one-key replay. Non-goals: scraping DRM streams, generating captions, or medical claims.
success_measure: At least 70% of pilot users report fewer than one manual replay per five minutes on a selected difficult clip.
monetization: one-time — the tool runs on user-provided caption files and has no ongoing service cost.
constraints: Only operate on captions the user can access; never claim to diagnose hearing loss; captions/transcripts remain local.
why_distinct: It improves comprehension of an existing caption track rather than competing as another transcription service.

title: Thought Parking
user: Adults with ADHD whose useful ideas interrupt current work and who need to capture them instantly without turning capture into task-planning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN received 141 comments on managing a constant stream of thoughts and ideas; replies describe the pull of the next shiny thought.
A user reports inconsistent microphone/dictation feedback across three capture surfaces, illustrating how even starting a quick capture can be cognitively disruptive.

recurrence: A high-comment ADHD request and a distinct dictation-friction report point to capture latency and attention switching, not a shortage of to-do lists.
current_workaround: Open a notes app, add an inbox task, send oneself a message, or try to remember the thought.
incumbents_and_gap: Todoist, Things, Obsidian, and voice dictation are capable general tools. Their capture flows invite categorization, reminders, and backlogs at the moment the user needs to return to work.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with a single full-screen hotkey/voice capture, no tags at capture time, deliberate review windows, and an archive-or-promote decision. Non-goals: task manager, coaching, calendar, or AI prioritization.
success_measure: In two weeks, users capture 20+ interruptions and return to their prior task within 30 seconds for at least 70% of captures.
monetization: one-time — private, offline capture has enduring but modest utility.
constraints: Voice clips and notes remain on device by default; accessibility settings must work before sign-in; do not make treatment or diagnostic claims.
why_distinct: The product deliberately postpones organization, which is the opposite of a conventional productivity inbox.

title: Meeting Recall Markers
user: Professionals with ADHD who lose the thread during meetings and need a private, low-effort way to reconstruct decisions and follow-ups afterward.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user explicitly asks what works for ADHD and focus during meetings.
The requester asks for a Lock In/ADHD Mode that hides non-critical distractions because they need to work rather than fall down product rabbit holes.

recurrence: Separate workplace and software-distraction requests show a recurring need to protect attention without adding more meeting machinery.
current_workaround: Take unstructured notes, record the whole meeting, ask a colleague afterward, or use a bot-based meeting transcription product.
incumbents_and_gap: Otter, Fireflies, and Teams transcripts create complete records; focus timers block time. Neither makes three tactile/keyboard markers—decision, action, revisit—the useful artifact without recording the meeting.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with three giant keyboard/touch markers and an optional 10-second personal voice note; it outputs a chronological recall card. Non-goals: meeting recording, speaker diarization, calendar integration, or AI summaries.
success_measure: At least 65% of pilot meetings yield a recall card that lets the user identify every personally assigned follow-up without replaying audio.
monetization: one-time — it is a private assistive aid rather than a team data platform.
constraints: No ambient audio capture by default; local storage and export only; provide reduced-motion and keyboard-only operation.
why_distinct: It captures attention anchors, not a surveillance-style transcript of everyone in the room.

title: Reading Resume
user: Dyslexic web readers who need to stop and resume a difficult passage at the exact sentence, with optional paced read-aloud support.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 2026 Show HN introduces a dyslexia-oriented Chrome TTS reader, evidence of an active need for browser-based supported reading.
The feature request asks for an optional dyslexia-friendly font stack in a local/offline e-ink reading workflow.

recurrence: Two separate reading workflows ask for dyslexia-aware support; font choice alone does not solve losing place after an interruption.
current_workaround: Change browser fonts, use a TTS extension, highlight manually, or reread several lines after every interruption.
incumbents_and_gap: OpenDyslexic fonts, Read&Write, and TTS readers improve presentation or audio. Few lightweight tools preserve a sentence-level return point across arbitrary articles while keeping visual and audio pacing synchronized.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension that saves a per-page sentence anchor, offers a configurable reading strip and device TTS from that anchor, then restores it after navigation. Non-goals: diagnosis, educational assessment, cloud accounts, or generating summaries.
success_measure: In a two-week pilot, users resume 80% of saved articles at the correct sentence without scrolling/searching.
monetization: one-time — local reading support should remain usable without a subscription.
constraints: Store anchors locally; do not claim fonts or TTS treat dyslexia; respect protected content and browser permissions.
why_distinct: The durable unit is an interruption-proof reading position, not another dyslexia font toggle.

title: Color Status Labeler
user: People with color-vision deficiency who need browser dashboards and maps to expose status without having to infer red/green or yellow/green meaning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker asks how people deal with color blindness; a reply says red/green deficiency prevents them from doing creative work or QA that depends on color appraisal.
A user requests a color-blind mode because the current state is simply "Everything is green or yellow."

recurrence: The same status-color ambiguity appears in both an end-user discussion and a product feature request, with work consequences for validation tasks.
current_workaround: Use OS color filters, ask another person, zoom in, or avoid color-dependent interfaces.
incumbents_and_gap: Color Oracle and browser simulators show how a page looks under a deficiency. They do not add a personal non-color legend or pattern overlay to the live status components the user must operate.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension with a user-trained picker: sample two or more recurring status colors on a site, assign labels/patterns, and overlay a compact legend on matching elements. Non-goals: certifying WCAG compliance, changing server data, or image editing.
success_measure: A pilot user configures two sites and correctly identifies 95% of a 20-state test without relying on hue alone.
monetization: free — the core should be broadly available; optional paid synced rule packs can be assessed only after adoption.
constraints: Rules stay local by default; avoid altering clicks or form values; clearly flag that pixel matching can be wrong after site redesigns.
why_distinct: It augments the user's live interface with redundant meaning instead of merely simulating a color-vision condition for designers.

title: No-Bot Captions
user: People who need real-time captions in Google Meet but cannot invite a recording bot into a meeting.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The user asks for real-time GMeet transcription specifically without meeting bots; a reply points to a client-side-only product.
A local transcription user reports that initial output can omit most of a sentence until they manually re-transcribe it, showing the need for visible recovery rather than blind trust.

recurrence: The privacy constraint is explicit, and a separate local-transcription report shows why a caption aid needs a rapid correction path.
current_workaround: Invite Otter/Fireflies-style bots, rely on platform captions, or record the meeting for later transcription.
incumbents_and_gap: Otter, Fireflies, and Meet captions offer transcription, but bot invitations create social/privacy friction and platform captions are not a portable, user-owned correction surface.
smallest_useful_product: A local desktop companion that captures only user-approved system audio, displays large rolling captions, marks dropped/uncertain segments, and lets the user replay the last 12 seconds. Non-goals: cloud storage, meeting attendance bots, speaker analytics, or hidden recording.
success_measure: In 20 captioned meetings, users recover an uncertain segment in under 15 seconds at least 90% of the time, with no bot participant added.
monetization: freemium — a local single-device mode can be free; paid installs can cover packaged offline models and support.
constraints: Obtain user consent and prominently show capture state; local model licensing must permit redistribution; never upload meeting audio by default.
why_distinct: It is a private caption display and repair loop, not a meeting intelligence bot.

title: Proper Noun Lexicon
user: People who rely on dictation or transcription for work and need names, acronyms, and company vocabulary rendered correctly without sharing an audio corpus.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN thread asks how to improve transcription accuracy for company names; replies discuss injecting specific terms into instructions.
The issue requests undo because cleanup can edit a user's words wrongly and currently offers no way to restore raw transcription.

recurrence: A direct vocabulary-accuracy question and an independent cleanup-error report show that post-hoc rewriting makes high-stakes names less trustworthy.
current_workaround: Repeat names, manually correct every transcript, add a long prompt, or accept a generic model's guess.
incumbents_and_gap: Whisper front ends and dictation apps may expose prompts or custom words, but usually do not offer a portable local lexicon with phonetic aliases, correction provenance, and a raw-text rollback.
smallest_useful_product: Local library/CLI plus compact review UI: import a CSV of approved terms and aliases, emit model-specific phrase bias/prompt files, and show a one-click raw-versus-corrected diff. Non-goals: training a speech model, cloud transcription, or automatic rewriting of unapproved names.
success_measure: On a pilot vocabulary of 100 names, the configured system improves exact-name recall by 25 percentage points while every correction remains reversible.
monetization: one-time — terminology is sensitive and users benefit from an offline tool they can keep.
constraints: Never transmit contact lists by default; support only documented model bias interfaces; preserve raw text and correction audit locally.
why_distinct: It is a portable, inspectable vocabulary layer rather than another speech-to-text model or LLM cleanup wrapper.

title: Quiet Dictation Bridge
user: People with motor, fatigue, or typing-access needs who work in open offices and need private push-to-talk dictation to their computer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The user asks how to use speech-to-text in an open office/co-working space and seeks a practical device recommendation.
The highly reacted request (263 reactions) asks for a mic push-to-talk control to dictate IDE prompts and follow-ups directly.

recurrence: An environmental privacy problem and a high-reaction push-to-talk request show that typing alternatives fail when the microphone is socially or acoustically unsuitable.
current_workaround: Whisper into a laptop, leave the room, use a headset dictation app, or type despite pain/fatigue.
incumbents_and_gap: Wispr Flow, Superwhisper, and OS dictation focus on a single device. They do not make a phone's close microphone a deliberate, local push-to-talk bridge to any paired desktop text field.
smallest_useful_product: Android phone app plus desktop receiver: hold-to-talk on the phone, locally transcribe on the phone or receiver, then paste only after a confirmation beep/haptic. Non-goals: always-listening assistant, cloud recording, LLM rewriting, or remote-device control.
success_measure: In an open-office pilot, 80% of dictated entries are accepted without a privacy-related retry and median end-to-end insertion is under three seconds.
monetization: one-time — the paired local utility has clear episodic purchase value and no service cost.
constraints: Use explicit pairing and encrypted local transport; show unmistakable recording state; use redistributable on-device STT or let users supply a model.
why_distinct: The novel unit is a private close-mic bridge, not a general dictation product or AI writing assistant.

title: Pronunciation Cards
user: Blind and low-vision screen-reader users reading technical material who need unfamiliar acronyms and names pronounced predictably in context.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Ask HN discussion about bad Apple transcription highlights that software jargon is common to a user but uncommon to a general speech system.
The requester proposes IPA pronunciation support in Edge Read Aloud specifically to improve accessibility for blind or visually impaired readers.

recurrence: Both reports expose a general-language model mismatch with personal and technical vocabulary; wrong pronunciation makes audio reading slower and harder to trust.
current_workaround: Spell terms manually, add ad-hoc pronunciation exceptions in one application, or switch to visual reading.
incumbents_and_gap: Edge Read Aloud and screen readers have dictionaries, but exceptions are app-specific and difficult to share with a document or team glossary.
smallest_useful_product: A local browser extension that detects user-selected terms, offers IPA/phonetic aliases and an audio preview, then applies the pronunciation via supported speech APIs or a copyable SSML reading card. Non-goals: automatic pronunciation guessing, voice cloning, or cloud TTS.
success_measure: Users configure 20 terms and report correct pronunciation for 90% of those terms across three supported reading surfaces.
monetization: free — interoperable accessibility metadata benefits from open adoption.
constraints: Use only documented browser speech capabilities; do not promise all screen readers accept injected pronunciation; keep glossaries local/exportable.
why_distinct: It treats pronunciation exceptions as portable reading metadata, rather than building another TTS engine.

title: Reading Comfort Pacer
user: Screen workers with eye fatigue who need reading breaks that occur at a natural stopping point instead of in the middle of a task.

evidence.quote_or_summary: People discuss eye-fatigue symptoms and workarounds; one reports difficulty focusing after extended close screen work and changes their desk setup for distance views.
A user requests configurable short and long eye-strain break warnings.

recurrence: Both an end-user health discussion and a product feature request identify sustained screen work and a need for interruptible reminders.
current_workaround: Set a timer, install a generic break reminder, ignore it when it interrupts, or use an OS focus mode.
incumbents_and_gap: LookAway, Stretchly, and OS reminders schedule time-based alerts. They do not wait for a user-confirmed paragraph/task boundary and offer a low-visual-load distance cue rather than another modal.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension with an accessible timer that requests a break only after the next user-triggered reading boundary, then shows a calm full-screen distance target and optional vibration. Non-goals: eye tracking, medical treatment, productivity surveillance, or health data collection.
success_measure: In 14 days, at least 60% of reminders are accepted or snoozed intentionally rather than dismissed, and users complete 10+ distance breaks.
monetization: free — basic ergonomic prompting should be freely available; avoid health-app dark patterns.
constraints: Make no medical claims; never access camera data; support reduced motion, screen readers, and a complete disable option.
why_distinct: It optimizes the interruption moment around reading flow instead of adding another rigid Pomodoro timer.

title: Hearing Mode Notes
user: Hearing-aid wearers who change listening modes by place and need a quick, private record of what setting actually worked.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN: Hearing aid wearers, what's hot? drew 210 comments, including discussion of AirPods as a possible backup rather than a replacement for primary hearing aids.
A hearing-aid user asks for volume control support after pairing AirPods hearing-aid mode with Android; they need access to listening modes and settings.

recurrence: A large wearer discussion and a concrete Android control request show that hearing support is highly contextual and hardware controls remain fragmented.
current_workaround: Memorize settings, take generic notes, repeatedly open a manufacturer app, or leave a suboptimal mode active.
incumbents_and_gap: Manufacturer companion apps expose device controls but rarely build a user-owned, cross-device memory of what worked in a restaurant, office, or commute. General note apps require too much setup in the moment.
smallest_useful_product: Offline Android app with one-tap place tags, mode/volume notes, optional manual sound-comfort rating, and a lock-screen reminder of the last successful setup. Non-goals: controlling hearing aids, sound amplification, hearing tests, or medical advice.
success_measure: After 30 days, users retrieve a prior successful setting in under 10 seconds for 70% of tagged places and report fewer trial-and-error changes.
monetization: one-time — personal accessibility notes should stay functional without subscription pressure.
constraints: No microphone access or health inference; location is optional and stored locally; never imply compatibility with or control over medical devices.
why_distinct: It is an experiential memory aid around device modes, not another hearing-aid controller or a medical app.
